title: Reunion with Nanda and Yashoda
story:
The caravan of the cowherds came slowly up the road — ox-carts, dusty men, the lowing of herds — and the Vrishnis who went out to meet it came back changed. In the middle of the crowd walked Nanda, older than when they had last seen him, and the Yadavas fell on him as if life itself had returned to their bodies. Vasudeva was the first to reach him. He embraced his old friend, pleased past all words, overwhelmed with love, holding on as a man holds on to something he thought he had lost. Around them the whole clan pressed close, hands reaching out, voices rising and falling, everyone talking at once and no one listening.

Then Krishna and Balarama came forward and bowed low to the two parents of their boyhood, to Nanda and Yashoda. With their own hands they seated the two parents on the seats of honor, and then, speechless with love, embraced them with both arms — the sons of Dwaraka holding the father and mother of Gokula, grown men who had commanded armies pressing their faces into shoulders they had not felt in years.

Yashoda took her two sons onto her lap. They were men now, broad-shouldered and scarred, princes of a city by the sea; on her lap they became again the boys who had crawled after the calves in her courtyard. She held them and said nothing, and the two of them let themselves be held. Around them the cowherds of Gokula stood smiling and wiping their eyes, as if they too had come home.

Then Devaki and Rohini came to Yashoda. The three women stood a moment, remembering. Devaki, who had given her sons into other hands when they were smaller than her arm, and Rohini, who had shared those first years of waiting — they embraced the queen of Vraja and spoke of the love she had shown the boys in Gokula. "Who could forget that friendship, queen of Vraja?" they said. "Who could forget what you gave them — the years of tending, the childhood you made safe and bright while we could only wait?" The boys, who had never known their parents' care until this day, had rested in her hands the way the eyelash rests on the eye — placed there, and safe, and afraid of nothing.

Yashoda answered them the way she had always answered: she gave them back their sons, sitting there on her lap, whole and grown. The two mothers of Dwaraka looked at the two boys of Gokula — at the princes everyone else in the field saw — and what they saw was the milkmaid's courtyard, the dust of the calf-pens, the little feet running in the sun. Nothing needed to be said about it. The embrace said it.

Vasudeva watched from a little way off and said nothing. Somewhere in his chest a debt he had never been able to name was being counted again, and he knew that before this gathering ended, he would have to speak of it. But not yet. Not while Yashoda's arms were still around her sons.

For the rest of that day, the eclipse field became a small Gokula again. The boys were back on their mother's lap; the years of separation had shrunk to nothing. The pilgrimage, which had begun as a duty under a darkened sun, ended with the oldest, simplest thing in the world: a mother holding her children, and the years falling away from her face. It was the kind of day the elders would tell about for years afterward — the day the whole family was whole again.
reflection: The quiet heart of the reunion is the meeting of the four mothers: Devaki and Rohini, who could not raise the boys, honour Yashoda, who did, and no one needs to say whose claim is greater. The embrace dissolves the old division between the two families in a single gesture.
next_story_tease: But the women of Vraja had come to the field too, and they had waited longest of all to see him.
hero_scene: Yashoda, seated on the pilgrimage ground, gathers both her grown sons onto her lap while Devaki and Rohini embrace her from either side, all three mothers weeping with joy as the cowherds of Gokula look on.
